description: we love space and we want to help astronauts with their well being in space
summary: AstroTwin is a health-monitoring prototype for astronauts that creates a live "digital twin" of every crew member. It combines readings from wearable sensors like those used on the ISS with real NASA data on cabin air, radiation and space weather. Today crew health data, environmental data and the medical team's view sit in separate places, so a slow decline can go unnoticed until it becomes serious. AstroTwin brings these streams together and compares each astronaut with their own normal values instead of a population average. It warns early, explains every alert in plain language and links changes to likely causes such as solar storms. A safety-checked assistant answers questions from NASA documents offline, cites its sources and never gives treatment instructions. The system includes three applications: one for the flight surgeon, a mobile app for each astronaut and a read-only copy for mission control on Earth. In simulated missions it caught 9 of 9 health episodes a median of three days early, with only 0.06 false alarms per 30 days. Its heart-rate measurements matched a standard reference tool to within 0.2 beats per minute, and it passes 121 automated tests. The next step is validation with real wearable data in analog missions.
details:
AstroTwin is an autonomous health-monitoring software designed for astronauts on space missions, operating independently offline. It bridges continuous biometric tracking with spacecraft subsystems to enable automated life-support responses. The project's core benefits include eliminating medical blind spots, providing real-time risk assessment, and delivering verified, protocol-backed clinical guidance without reliance on ground control. Its intended impact is safeguarding crew health and enhancing mission survivability in deep space.

Technically, AstroTwin is built using FastAPI v2, SQLite, and Python libraries (numpy, scipy) at the edge, alongside anomaly-detection models (Isolation Forest, autoencoders), a hybrid RAG architecture utilizing Gemma 3:4b via Ollama, Streamlit for mission/crew consoles, and Flutter for the mobile app.

The project demonstrates creativity through sex-specific biometric calibration—accounting for physiological baseline differences between male and female astronauts—and dual-purpose feedback reports optimized for both live mission operations and post-mission readiness. During development, the team considered rigorous aerospace standards (such as NASA protocols and literature), latency constraints in deep space communications, data privacy, and reliability validated through Living Lab simulations.
